newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr unnerved as bell tolls for BOJ rates.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr unnerved as bell tolls for BOJ rates.

text.p: The Australian dollar sagged against the yen Wednesday as key Japanese economic data proved so unexpectedly upbeat they could just herald the first policy tightening since August 1990.
The Bank of Japan's influential Tankan survey of business sentiment showed industry was in far better spirits than anyone imagined and money markets quickly moved to price in a hike.

Analysts cautioned the recovery was too un-even for the BOJ to move soon, but said the data had clearly focused minds on the risk. Narrrowing yield differentials would hurt AUD/yen short term, but Japanese growth should actually be bullish over time.

That was because Japan was easily the largest consumer of Australian commodities and stronger economic growth there typically led to greater demand for, and prices of, Australian exports like coal and copper.

This prospect may have helped keep the dollar steady at US$0.7509/14 by 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) from an early US$0.7501/06. That was off from Tuesday's late US$0.7518/23 but well within the US$0.7470/7540 range held since the start of last week.
The rise in Japanese yields was real and immediate, however, and saw the local currency slapped down to 85.20/30 yen from 86.05/15 just before the data hit dealing screens.

In this it mirrored the U.S. dollar which sank to 113.30 yen from 114.80 as the market contemplated the end of the BOJ's ultra-easy policy stance. The discount rate was cut to a 0.5 percent low in September 1995 as the culmination of an easing process begun in July 1991 when rates stood at 6.0 percent.
The market always knew rates would have to turn higher eventually but had thought the BOJ would hold off until at least the first quarter of next year.
The Tankan looked to have changed that, with the new betting seen in the December 3-month Euroyen futures contract which leapt 15 basis points to 99.00, implying a rate of 1.00 percent.
And the June contract leapt 21 basis points to 98.52, suggesting scope for a full one point ODR hike in the next year.
The Tankan's main diffusion index for large manufacturing firms showing a reading of plus 7.0 in June against plus 2.0 in March and expectations of a slight fall.
The shock was all the greater since the market had been lulled by rumours the June survey would be depressed by the economic volatility surrounding a hike in VAT rates in April.
Instead, manufacturing industry was more confident than at any time since 1991 and the improvement was expected to last with the BOJ forecasting a diffusion index of plus 8.0 for Q3.
The improvement was far from universal, however, and owed much to export growth while domestic demand had turned lower after the VAT hike.
The sentiment index for non-manufacturing actually eased to minus 8.0 from minus 7.0 in March and that for small firms improved only marginally to minus 7.0 from minus 8.0.

"The Tankan highlights the continued lop-sided nature of Japan's economic recovery," said Bankers Trust economist David Bassanese. "The strong showing by manufacturers does incresae the chance of a hike later this year, but the authorities may want to first see if the outlook for other sectors improves."
And a stronger Japanese economy had positive implications for commodity prices which could compensate the A$ for narrowing yield differentials in the longer run.

The mechanism was evident in the fact the main Tankan diffusion index had a good historical correlation with the Reserve Bank's index of commodity prices, which covers all of the country's major commodity exports.
If that relationship held true, the decisive rise in the June Tankan promised to lift commodity prices to the benefit of the A$.
